All Bs speech varieties except some dialects of Kuy and Tsg retain phonemic accent. tone_statements.citation: Zorc, R. David. 1993. Overview of Austronesian and Philippine accent patterns. In Jerold A. Edmondson and Kenneth J. Gregerson (eds.), Tonality in Austronesian Languages (Oceanic Linguistics Special Publication No. 24), 17-24. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press.
tone_statements.quote: [p.18] Both word accent and intonation involve three details: 1) long vs short vowels (length), 2) pitch or high vs low tones (pitch accent), 3) loudness or amplitude (stress). ... In Philippine languages, vowel length (or shortness) is the most important feature of word accent ... [p.19, sec. 3] In all Philippine languages stress or pitch accent is a syntactic (grammatical) feature, a means of indicating an accent group (phrase); it does not even necessarily coincide with length. ... [p.20, Table 2] (A) Phonemic length and shortness, as inherited from PPH (< PHN, PMP, PAN): Bisayan (except Kuyonon and Tausug), Coastal and Pandan Bikol, ...
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2 p. 18; sec. 3 'Stress accent as a grammatical feature' p. 19; sec. 6 Table 2 'Accent classification of Austronesian languages', class (A), p. 20
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone: pitch (high/low) and stress function at the phrase level as accent-group/intonation marking in all Philippine languages; the lexical contrast is word accent realized primarily as vowel length, phonemic and inherited in Bisayan (Kuyonon and Tausug excepted); accent also used morphemically in most Central Philippine languages.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every deciding fragment is in the Zorc 1977 PDF we hold/scanned layer at the stated pages (pp.50-51, 216, 218, 243; dialect entry 24 Naturalis = Tandag & Tago). The classification (lexical accent, penult vs ultima on open-penult roots; closed penult always penult-accented) rests on a 1977 comparative-historical monograph whose accent claims are framed for 'all Bs dialects' with Naturalis in the 36-dialect field sample, which is second-best to a dedicated description -- but the ISO 639-3 change request (SIL 2009) and Glottolog agree that no other description of Tandaganon exists, and Lobel 2013 (checked) is silent on its stress. Dumanig 2015 on sister Surigaonon, downloaded now, independently shows the same contrastive penult/final stress with minimal pairs. Nothing suggests the classification is wrong; the best available source is held and quoted, so status 'adequate' (not 'well-source

sources.citation: Dumanig, Francisco Perlas. 2015. Descriptive analysis of the Surigaonon language. Polyglossia 27: 1-10. doi:10.34382/00011430 (Ritsumeikan APU repository, open)
sources.quote: 'The stress in Surigaonon is indicated by an apostrophe where the stressed syllable is always given more emphasis by increasing the pitch and loudness. In some cases, the change of stressed syllable also changes the meaning of the word' -- Table 6 lists penult- vs final-stressed minimal pairs (búyag 'separate (adj.)' vs buyág 'to separate', ámo 'master' vs amó? 'monkey', úban 'white hair' vs ubán 'accompany', etc.). Describes Surigaonon (Surigao del Norte), the sister variety from which Tandaganon was split in ISO 2009-087, not Tandaganon itself; corroborates lexical penult/ultima stress contr

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority / Hall, Bill (SIL). 2009. Change Request 2009-087 (split [sul], create [tgn] Tandaganon), request form + new-code form.
sources.quote: No stress statement. Bibliographically decisive: 'Zorc treats Tandaganon (his "Naturalis") as coordinate with Surigaonon ... there is no literature or research other than Zorc and Lobel that has treated Tandaganon at all.' Confirms the Naturalis = Tandaganon identity our record relies on and that Zorc 1977 is the only substantive source.
